extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and general readers interested in narrative technique and narratology
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of narration choices (who tells the story and how) including point of view, tense, and narrative techniques used to present fiction and other narrative forms. Useful as guidance for choosing and evaluating narrative voice, perspective, and methods in creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is the use of a written or spoken commentary to convey a story to an audience; it is conveyed by a narrator who delivers information about the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration presents the story in its entirety and is a required element of written stories (novels, short stories, poems, memoirs, etc.). It is optional in many other storytelling formats (films, plays, television, video games) where story can be conveyed through dialogue or visual action. Consider whether your work needs explicit narration or can rely on other means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mode (point of view / perspective / voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative mode encompasses choices used to develop the narrator and narration: narrative point of view, perspective, or voice — the choice of grammatical person used by the narrator and the scope of information the narrator presents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a narrative mode determines the narrator's relation to events and audience (participant vs. outsider) and controls what information is available. Use the mode deliberately to shape reader intimacy, reliability, and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative tense
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of either the past or present grammatical tense to establish either the prior completion or current immediacy of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past tense is far more common and can be distant or immediate; present tense gives a sense of immediacy and is common in conversational narratives and some modern novels; the historical present can narrate past events as if current. Future tense is rare and often gives a prophetic tone. Screenplay action is written in present tense. Choose tense to match tone and desired immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative technique (other methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any of the various other methods chosen to help narrate a story, such as establishing the story's setting, developing characters, exploring themes, structuring the plot, intentionally expressing certain details but not others, following or subverting genre norms, employing certain linguistic styles and using various other storytelling devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include framing, flashback/flashforward, stream-of-consciousness, unreliable narration, and many stylistic devices. Combine techniques to achieve thematic and affective goals; be mindful of genre expectations if you intend to follow or subvert norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-person point of view reveals the story through an openly self-referential and participating narrator; it uses pronouns like I and me (and we/us) and creates a close relationship between narrator and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person provides intimacy and direct access to the narrator's perceptions and voice; it can increase bias and unreliability. Consider whether the narrator is an eyewitness, participant, or later reteller and how that affects trust and scope of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-person uses the second-person pronoun you; it can recount experience while adding distance or irony and can produce unreliability. In some media (gamebooks, interactive fiction), addressed-reader devices may resemble but are not strictly true second-person narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-person can create immediacy or alienation; use sparingly and purposefully. Note distinctions in interactive formats where an implicit narrator/writer addresses a player rather than a true second-person narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In third-person narration the narration refers to all characters with third-person pronouns like he or she and never first- or second-person pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person is versatile and can range from close focalization on one character to fully omniscient viewpoints. Decide how tightly the narrator is aligned with a character's consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omniscient vs. limited (close) perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Omniscient point of view is presented by a narrator with an overarching perspective, seeing and knowing everything that happens within the world of the story, including what each character is thinking and feeling. Limited or close third-person is confined to one character's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omniscience allows broad world knowledge and authorial commentary (typical in 19th-century fiction); limited/close third-person gives depth to one character's inner life while maintaining third-person distance. Choose based on whether you need sweeping scope or focused intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective vs. objective point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective point of view conveys the thoughts, feelings and opinions of one or more characters. Objective point of view employs a narrator who tells a story without describing any character's thoughts, opinions, or feelings, giving an objective, unbiased point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective narration gives internal access and colored interpretation; objective narration reports observable actions and dialogue without interiority, which can create distance or ambiguity. Use objective narration to let readers infer inner states; use subjective to shape empathy and perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating or multiple narrators (multiperspectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works employ multiple points of view, alternating between different first-person narrators or alternating between first- and third-person modes; multiperspectivity presents different characters' storylines and can illustrate complex social identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple narrators can reveal contrasts, biases, and differing knowledge; frame stories and enclosed narratives (e.g., One Thousand and One Nights) use nested narration. Use clear signals for perspective shifts to avoid reader confusion and to exploit interpretive contrasts among narrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planes of point of view (Uspensky / Lanser)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boris Uspenskij identifies five planes on which point of view is expressed: spatial, temporal, psychological, phraseological and ideological. Susan Lanser develops similar categories; psychological point of view focuses on characters' behaviors and the narrator's distance/affinity, while ideological point of view focuses on norms, values and worldview (may be explicit or embedded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing point of view, consider not only person and tense but how spatial/temporal focalization, language choices (phraseology), psychological closeness, and ideological stance shape interpretation. Ideology may be explicit or hidden at deep-structural levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense variation and special uses (historical present, screenplay, prophetic future)
rubrics_metrics.description: Past tense is most common; present tense depicts events as occurring now and can give immediacy; historical present narrates past events in present tense. Screenplay action uses present tense. Future tense is rare and often conveys a prophetic tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how tense affects reader perception of time and authority. Use present for immediacy or conversational tone; use past for traditional narrative distance; use future sparingly for foreknowledge or prophecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream of consciousness attempts to replicate the thought processes of the narrative character (often first-person), including interior monologues, incomplete thoughts, and fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique gives raw interior access and associative flow; it's demanding for readers and best used when the interior perspective is central to the work. Examples include Joyce and Faulkner; apply carefully to avoid incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narration uses an untrustworthy narrator to give the audience a deliberate sense of disbelief or suspicion about what is true. Unreliable narrators are usually first-person but can be third-person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unreliability to create mystery, irony, or thematic complexity. Signal unreliability subtly (biases, contradictions, omissions) and decide whether and how the truth is eventually revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and oral/multiple-teller traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing devices (story within a story) and traditions of multiple elders/narrators (oral storytelling) shape how tales are related and can produce countless variations tailored to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use framing to connect discrete tales, provide commentary, or modulate narrative distance. Consider cultural storytelling practices (e.g., elders adapting tales) when designing narratorial plurality and variation for different audiences.
